query: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a simple solid-solution state has favorable plasticity and machinability but relatively low hardness and strength, while its deformation behavior remains poorly understood. Under mechanical-property and deformation testing, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs this low hardness and strength and why? Define a controlled comparison, predict the observations relative to the starting state, state the applicable composition, structural-state, and loading boundaries, connect the hypothesis to the reported property combination, and specify a falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: The low hardness and strength of equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi high-entropy alloys in a simple solid-solution state are governed by the character and distribution of grain boundaries, which influence the deformation behavior by controlling the movement of dislocations and the formation of deformation twins.
generation.material_initial_state: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi high-entropy alloy in a simple solid-solution state
generation.intervention: Controlled variation of grain boundary character and distribution

generation.mechanism: Influence of grain boundaries on dislocation movement and deformation twin formation
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with a higher fraction of low-angle grain boundaries and a more uniform distribution of grain boundary character will exhibit higher hardness and strength compared to those with a higher fraction of high-angle grain boundaries and a more random distribution of grain boundary character
generation.baseline: As-cast or annealed equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi high-entropy alloy with a random distribution of grain boundary character
